metadata.title: PISA reading achievement: identifying predictors and examining model generalizability for multilingual students

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the U.S. 2018 PISA reading assessment microdata (students aged 15–16) and applies the student sampling weight in analyses involving plausible values and multilevel modeling. In the elastic net variable-selection step, the overall student sampling weight is included, and in the multilevel modeling step the sampling weights are included and scaled before estimation. The authors do not report replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty quantification is described through model-based standard errors and likelihood-ratio tests rather than replicate-based variance estimation. Because the analysis is multilevel and uses PVs, the weighting is intended to better reflect the target population within the complex survey design, but the paper does not provide the exact weight variable name in the excerpt.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the U.S. PISA 2018 reading assessment student sample aged 15–16, including student, teacher, and school questionnaires. The analytic sample excludes 48 students (1%) who did not report language status; multilingual (ML) and monolingual (MN) subsamples are then defined by reported language status. For variable selection and modeling, variables with missing proportion above 20% were excluded, and remaining missing values were imputed using predictive mean matching (elastic net step) and fully conditional specification (FCS) within mice/miceadds (multilevel modeling step). Teacher variables were aggregated to the school level because students are nested within schools and associated with more than one teacher, making a teacher-nesting level infeasible.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel modeling with PVs (10 PV sets). Model fit improved: Model 1 vs Model 0 F(11, 479)=221.97, p<.001; Model 3 vs Model 2 F(10, 208400)=3.755, p<.001. Variance explained: L1 R²=0.44; L2 R²=0.11. ICC (Model 0) =0.29 (17.4% variance at teacher+school levels).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data (U.S., grades 10–11) the study leveraged Test effort, ISCED educational level, Grade repetition, Books at home, and Reading self-efficacy to predict Reading achievement (PVs), finding that Grade repetition had a significant negative association (b=-26.33, β=-0.07, p<.001) while multiple student-level factors (e.g., effort, ISCED level, books at home, digital affordance, metacognition, self-efficacy, peer interaction, instructional support) showed significant positive associations. This indicates that strengthening instructionally malleable reading supports (self-efficacy, metacognition, peer-supportive environments) and reducing grade retention/attendance problems may improve high-school reading outcomes, especially for multilingual learners, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (U.S., multilingual students, grade 10–11, age 15–16)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel modeling with PVs. ML vs MN generalizability results reported via full model parameter estimates (Table 6). For ML students: Grade repetition b=-42.54, β=-0.14, p<.001; Self-efficacy b=20.63, β=0.20, p<.001; Peer interaction b=21.55, β=0.19, p<.001; Extracurricular literacy b=3.24, β=0.10, p=.04. Perceptions of instructional support was not significant for ML (b=5.11, β=0.05, p=.16).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading data for multilingual students (U.S., grades 10–11) the study leveraged Grade repetition, Reading self-efficacy, Peer interaction, Extracurricular literacy, and Perceptions of instructional support to predict Reading achievement (PVs), finding that Grade repetition was substantially more negative for ML students (b=-42.54, β=-0.14) while self-efficacy and peer interaction were stronger positive correlates (self-efficacy b=20.63, β=0.20; peer interaction b=21.55, β=0.19). This indicates that multilingual students may benefit more from policies that prevent grade retention and from school/community literacy opportunities that build supportive peer networks and reading confidence, while teacher-instruction support as perceived by students may not translate into measurable achievement gains in this cross-sectional snapshot.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes U.S. PISA 2018 reading achievement for students aged 15–16 (grades 10–11), using the 10 plausible values (PVs) for reading and applying student sampling weights in both the elastic net variable-selection stage and the subsequent multilevel modeling. The authors first use Elastic Net (implemented in R via caret and glmnet) to rank and select salient predictors across student, teacher, and school levels, excluding variables with >20% missingness and imputing missing data (predictive mean matching for selection; FCS with mice/miceadds for modeling). In the full U.S. sample (N=4,838), multilevel models show that student-level variables explain 44% of level-1 variance and teacher/school-level variables explain 11% of level-2 variance, with grade repetition negatively associated and multiple reading-related psychosocial and home resources positively associated. For multilingual students (N=736), grade repetition is more strongly negative and self-efficacy and peer interaction are stronger positive correlates; extracurricular literacy is uniquely significant for ML students. Limitations include cross-sectional PV-based achievement, no causal identification, and no replicate-weight reporting in the excerpt.
